title: Cheapest Network
statement:
A provider wants to connect **n** villages with fibre cables so that every village can reach every other village (directly or through other villages). There are **m** possible cables; cable i would connect villages u and v and costs w.

Find the minimum total cost to connect all villages, or print -1 if it is impossible even when building every cable.
input:
The first line contains two integers **n** and **m**.

Each of the next m lines contains three integers u, v and w. Several cables may connect the same pair of villages.
output: Print one integer: the minimum total cost, or -1. If n = 1, nothing needs to be built and the answer is 0.
hints: This is a minimum spanning tree. Kruskal's algorithm is greedy: try the cables from cheapest to most expensive.
Take a cable only if it connects two villages that are not connected yet. A Disjoint Set Union (union-find) answers that quickly.
If fewer than n - 1 cables were taken, the villages cannot all be connected. The total needs 64 bits.
editorial:
Kruskal's algorithm. Sort the cables by cost. Go through them in that order and use union-find: if u and v are in different components, build the cable (add its cost, unite the components); otherwise skip it, because it would only close a cycle. The greedy choice is safe: the cheapest cable crossing any cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree. At the end, if exactly n - 1 cables were taken, print the total, otherwise -1. Use path compression (and optionally union by size).

Complexity: O(m log m).
